entry: Form of government in which the state, or a network of social institutions, protects and promotes the [[Well-being|well-being]] of its citizens. Welfare states rest on equal opportunity, equitable distribution of wealth and public responsibility for citizens unable to avail themselves of minimal provisions for a good life. Early features, such as public [[Pension|pensions]] and social insurance, developed from the 1880s in industrializing Western countries. Emperor [[Ashoka]] of India put forward an idea of a welfare state in the 3rd century BCE. The term was popularized during World War II by Anglican archbishop William Temple, and the fullest forms were developed after [[World War II]]. Comparisons of income before and after [[Tax|taxes]] and transfers show reductions in relative poverty of 20–28 percentage points in high-spending nations such as Finland and France. Critics argue that welfare systems can distort labor markets, foster dependency and impede economic growth.

Excavation or structure made by digging, driving or drilling to access liquid resources, usually water. The oldest and most common kind is the water well, which taps [[Groundwater|groundwater]] in underground [[Aquifer|aquifers]] and is drawn up by a pump or by containers raised by hand. Wells were first constructed at least eight thousand years ago, and linings of wood or wickerwork date back at least to the Iron Age. Traditional dug wells are still sunk by hand in rural areas of the developing world, often lined with brick or stone. Deeper wells are [[Drilling|drilled]] and usually cased with [[Steel|steel]] or [[Plastic|plastic]] pipe, reaching much greater depths than dug wells. Well water typically contains more dissolved minerals than surface water and may require treatment before it is potable. Soil salination can occur as the water table falls, and methane can seep into the water.

Measure of how well a person's life is going, also called welfare or quality of life. Well-being is what is intrinsically good for a person, and it contrasts with ill-being, which denotes negative conditions. Researchers distinguish subjective well-being, how a person feels about and evaluates their life, from objective well-being, which includes [[Health|health]], income and security. [[Hedonism]] holds that well-being depends on the balance of pleasure over pain, desire theories locate it in satisfied desires, and objective list theories combine diverse elements. Often discussed factors include [[Emotion|emotions]], life satisfaction, achievement, a sense of meaning, [[Interpersonal relationship|interpersonal relationships]] and health. It is studied in [[Philosophy|philosophy]], economics, psychology, sociology and medicine. Empirical research has intensified only since the second half of the 20th century.

Capital city of [[New Zealand]], at the southwestern tip of the [[North Island]] between [[Cook Strait]] and the Remutaka Range. It is the world's southernmost capital of a sovereign state, and it has been the seat of government since 1865, a status set by convention rather than legislation. The city is the center of New Zealand's film and special effects industries and a leading financial center in the Asia-Pacific region. Often called New Zealand's cultural capital, it is also the world's windiest city by average wind speed.

Brittonic Celtic language native to the Welsh people, historically also known as Cambrian, Cambric and Cymric. Known natively as *Cymraeg*, it is spoken by about 18% of the population of [[Wales]], by some in [[England]], and in the Welsh colony of *Y Wladfa* in Chubut Province, [[Argentina]]. Welsh and English are official languages of the Senedd, the Welsh parliament. The 2021 census counted 538,300 residents aged three or over (17.8% of the population) able to speak Welsh. The Welsh Government plans to reach one million speakers by 2050. [[UNESCO]] considers Welsh the least endangered Celtic language.

[[Association football]] stadium in Wembley, London, England. Opened in 2007 on the site of the original stadium, it is England's national stadium and hosts most England home matches and the FA Cup final. With 90,000 seats, it is the largest stadium in the UK and the second-largest in Europe, behind Barcelona's Camp Nou. The 134-meter-high (440 ft) Wembley Arch supports over 75% of the roof load. It hosted the 2011, 2013 and 2024 [[UEFA]] Champions League finals and the 2012 Olympic football gold-medal matches. It was the temporary home of [[Premier League]] club Tottenham Hotspur from 2017 to 2019.

Mythological creature or evil spirit from Algonquian folklore, sometimes depicted as a [[Giant|giant]] humanoid with a heart of ice. The wendigo is said to possess humans and to cause insatiable hunger, a desire to eat other humans and a propensity to murder. Associated with the north, winter, cold and [[Famine|famine]], it has been widely used in literature and [[Horror fiction|horror fiction]]. Algernon Blackwood popularized the English form in his 1910 novella *The Wendigo*. In [[Psychiatry|psychiatry]], wendigo psychosis is a culture-bound syndrome marked by an intense craving for human flesh and a fear of becoming a cannibal.

Mythological human able to transform into a wolf, typically under a curse or other affliction. The word derives from Old English *wer(e)wulf*, meaning man-wolf, and the alternative term lycanthrope comes from Ancient Greek. Belief in werewolves developed alongside belief in [[Witchcraft|witches]] during the late [[Middle Ages]] and early modern period. Trials of supposed werewolves began in what is now Switzerland in the early 15th century and peaked in the 17th century. Hundreds of people were executed across Europe on werewolf charges between 1520 and 1630. In Greek legend, [[Zeus]] transformed King Lycaon of Arcadia into a wolf. Modern films often show transformations triggered by the [[Full moon|full moon]] and transmitted by a bite.

German theoretical physicist, a pioneer of [[Quantum mechanics]] and a principal scientist in Germany's nuclear program during [[World War II]]. In 1925 he reinterpreted old quantum theory and, with [[Max Born]] and Pascual Jordan, substantially elaborated the [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] formulation of quantum mechanics. He introduced the [[Uncertainty principle]] in 1927 and received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1932 for the creation of quantum mechanics. His work also covered [[Atomic nucleus|atomic nuclei]], [[Cosmic ray|cosmic rays]], [[Subatomic particle|subatomic particles]], turbulence and ferromagnetism. After the war he directed the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics, later renamed the Max Planck Institute, until it moved to Munich in 1958. Debate continues over whether his nuclear program failed to produce a bomb through deliberate obstruction, calculation errors or insurmountable constraints.

German filmmaker, actor, opera director and author, regarded as a pioneer of New German Cinema. His films often feature ambitious protagonists, people with unusual talents, or individuals in conflict with nature, and he avoids storyboards in favor of improvisation. He directed [[Klaus Kinski]] in *Aguirre, the Wrath of God* (1972), *Nosferatu the Vampyre* and *Woyzeck* (both 1979), *Fitzcarraldo* (1982) and *Cobra Verde* (1987). His documentaries include *Grizzly Man* (2005) and *Cave of Forgotten Dreams* (2010). He has directed more than two dozen operas and published over 12 books. He has won four awards at the [[Cannes Film Festival]]. Critic [[Roger Ebert]] said he had never made a film that was compromised, shameful or uninteresting, and [[François Truffaut]] called him the most important film director alive.

German-American aerospace engineer and space architect who led German rocket technology in World War II. He co-developed the [[V-2 rocket|V-2]] at Peenemünde, and the V-2 became the first artificial object to cross the [[Kármán line]], on 20 June 1944. He had joined the [[Nazi Party]] and later the Allgemeine SS. After the war about 1,600 German scientists, engineers and technicians were brought to the United States under [[Operation Paperclip]], and he developed the rockets that launched Explorer 1 in 1958. In 1960 his group joined [[NASA]], where he directed the Marshall Space Flight Center and was chief architect of the [[Saturn V]] that carried the [[Apollo program|Apollo]] spacecraft to the Moon. Some see him as having escaped justice for Nazi war crimes, given American competition with the Soviets during the Cold War.

American filmmaker from [[Houston]], known for films about grief, loss of innocence and dysfunctional families. Critics call him an auteur for his eccentric style. His early films *Bottle Rocket* (1996) and *Rushmore* (1998) were followed by *The Royal Tenenbaums* (2001) and *The Grand Budapest Hotel* (2014), which earned his first Academy Award nominations for Best Director and Best Picture. *Fantastic Mr. Fox* (2009), an adaptation of [[Roald Dahl]]'s book, and *Isle of Dogs* (2018) are stop-motion films. He won the Academy Award for Best Live Action Short Film for *The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar* (2023).

American filmmaker, best known for horror and especially [[Slasher film|slasher films]] that mixed horror clichés with humor. He created the *A Nightmare on Elm Street* franchise, writing and directing its first film in 1984. He directed the first four films of the *Scream* franchise (1996–2011), along with the cult films *The Last House on the Left* (1972) and *The Hills Have Eyes* (1977). His other films include *Swamp Thing* (1982) and the horror comedy *The People Under the Stairs* (1991). In 1995 he received a Life Career Award from the Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror Films, which honors the [[Horror film|horror genre]].

Anglo-Saxon kingdom in southern [[Great Britain]], also known as the Kingdom of the West Saxons, from around 519 to around 927. Wessex became Christian after Cenwalh was baptized, and under Ine it issued one of the oldest surviving English law codes. [[Alfred the Great]] adopted the title King of the [[Anglo-Saxons]] in about 886 and defended the kingdom against Danish invasions. His grandson [[Æthelstan]] conquered York, the last surviving Danish kingdom, in 927. [[Cnut]] later created the wealthy earldom of Wessex, but in 1066 Harold Godwinson reunited the earldom with the crown, and Wessex ceased to exist.

Westernmost region of Africa, defined by the United Nations as sixteen countries with a population of 419 million as of 2021. [[Nigeria]] is the most populous country in Africa, with more than 242 million people. Historically the region held powerful states such as the Mali and Gao Empires, which controlled trade in goods such as gold, ivory and advanced iron-working. As European exploration incorporated local economies into the [[Atlantic slave trade]], it expanded existing [[Slavery|slavery]]. Colonial powers, especially France and Britain, continued to exploit the region after the early 19th-century end of the slave trade. The climate is shaped by the [[Sahara]] to the north and by Atlantic monsoons, supporting biomes from forests to drylands. Threats include [[Deforestation]], biodiversity loss, overfishing and pollution from mining.

Westernmost region of [[Asia]], also called Western Asia or Southwest Asia. As defined by most academics, it comprises [[Anatolia]], the [[Arabian Peninsula]], Iran, [[Mesopotamia]], the Armenian highlands, the [[Levant]], the Sinai Peninsula and the South Caucasus. It is separated from Africa by the Isthmus of Suez and from Europe by the Turkish Straits. The region contains most of the Middle East and has a population of about 313 million. Its most populous countries are Iran, Turkey, Iraq, Yemen and Saudi Arabia. Definitions vary across institutions, and none is generally accepted. The region is the cradle of ancient civilizations such as Sumer and Akkad, and of [[Judaism]], [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]].

Landlocked Palestinian territory west of the [[Jordan River]], occupied by [[Israel]] since the [[Six-Day War]] of 1967. It is the larger of the two Palestinian territories, the other being the [[Gaza Strip]]. Jordan had annexed the area after the [[1948 Arab–Israeli War]]. The mid-1990s [[Oslo Accords]] divided it into three areas, with Israel controlling Area C, about 60% of the territory. In 2024 the [[International Court of Justice]] ruled again that Israel's occupation is unlawful. Palestinians regard the West Bank as the heart of their envisaged state, while many right-wing and religious Israelis regard it as their ancestral homeland.

State in eastern [[India]] on the Bay of Bengal, with [[Kolkata]] as its capital. It was formed in 1947 by the [[Partition of India|partition]] of Bengal along religious lines, and it borders [[Bangladesh]] to the east and Nepal and Bhutan to the north. Its population was around 91 million in 2011, making it India's fourth-most populous state. The region was a center of the [[Indian independence movement]] and of the 19th-century Bengal Renaissance, which spurred reforms in education and social customs. Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore was among its best-known cultural figures. After communist rule began in 1977, the state endured political violence and economic stagnation before it rebounded. Its economy rests on agriculture and small and medium-sized enterprises, and it has three World Heritage sites.

Mainstream professional theater staged in the large theaters in and near London's West End. It is the highest level of commercial theater in the United Kingdom and, with [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]], in the English-speaking world. About 40 theaters operate in the West End, the oldest being the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, which opened in 1663. Audiences reached a record 17.1 million in 2023. Theater flourished in London after the Reformation until the [[Puritans]] closed the theaters in 1642. After the Restoration of 1660, the first West End theater was built, and [[Christopher Wren]] later designed its replacement. The Laurence Olivier Awards honor professional London theater, including West End productions.

Common English name for the Federal Republic of Germany from 1949 until its reunification with East Germany in 1990. Known as the Bonn Republic after its capital, it belonged to the Western Bloc during the [[Cold War]]. Under Chancellor [[Konrad Adenauer]], who served until 1963, it aligned fully with [[NATO]]. Its economic recovery in the 1950s, the Wirtschaftswunder, made it the world's second-largest economy. East Germany acceded to the federal republic in 1990 after the opening of the [[Berlin Wall]], and the reunited state kept West Germany's international memberships.

Freshwater lake in [[Hangzhou]], [[China]], lying west of the city's former walls. Also known as Xihu, it covers 6.39 square kilometers and contains four causeways and three artificial islands. It has been a tourist attraction since the [[Tang dynasty]], and by the [[Song dynasty]] it was a cultural landmark. Bai Juyi was among the first to call it West Lake, and [[Su Shi]] used the name in official documents when he requested dredging in 1090. A [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] since 2011, it is recognized as an influence on garden design in China, Japan and Korea. It was the first major Chinese tourist attraction to cancel admission fees.

Human disease caused by infection with the West Nile virus, which is usually spread by [[Mosquito|mosquitoes]]. About 80% of infections cause few or no symptoms, and about 20% cause fever, headache, vomiting or a rash. In less than 1% of people, [[Encephalitis|encephalitis]] or [[Meningitis|meningitis]] occurs, and the risk of death among those with nervous system involvement is about 10%. Severe disease is most likely in people over 60 and in those with weak immune systems. The virus was discovered in [[Uganda]] in 1937 and first detected in North America in 1999. There is no human [[Vaccine|vaccine]] and no specific treatment, so prevention relies on avoiding mosquito bites and eliminating standing water.

Large plain occupying western [[Siberia]], between the [[Ural Mountains]] and the [[Yenisei]] River. It is described as the world's largest unbroken lowland, with more than half its area less than 100 meters (328 ft) above sea level. Much of it is poorly drained, with some of the world's largest swamps, floodplains and bogs, including the Vasyugan Swamp, one of the world's largest single raised bogs. The climate is subarctic or continental, with harsh, long winters. Vegetation ranges from [[Tundra]] in the north to steppe in the south, and [[Permafrost]] is present in the north. The plain holds large [[Petroleum|petroleum]] and [[Natural gas|natural gas]] reserves, and most of Russia's oil and gas production came from it in the 1970s and 1980s.

Musical by [[Leonard Bernstein]] and [[Stephen Sondheim]], inspired by [[Romeo and Juliet]] by [[William Shakespeare]]. Set in the mid-1950s on Manhattan's Upper West Side, it follows the rivalry between the Jets, a white street gang, and the Sharks, recent migrants from Puerto Rico. Tony, a former Jet, falls in love with Maria, sister of the Sharks' leader. Its dark themes, sophisticated score and extended dance scenes marked a turning point in [[Musical theatre|musical theater]]. The original 1957 Broadway production ran for 732 performances and marked Sondheim's Broadway debut. The 1961 film adaptation won ten of its eleven Academy Award nominations, including Best Picture, and a 2021 film directed by [[Steven Spielberg]] was also nominated for Best Picture.

Mountainous, landlocked state in the Southern and Mid-Atlantic regions of the United States. It was admitted to the Union on June 20, 1863, during the [[American Civil War]], as a slave state, after some Virginia counties refused to secede. It is the only state formed by separating from a Confederate state. Its [[Coal|coalfields]] made it a leading producer by the early 20th century. It voted heavily for the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] from the Great Depression to the 1990s and has since become heavily Republican. It is the only state entirely within the [[Appalachia|Appalachian]] region.
